A content delivery network exists to make websites and videos load quickly no matter where a person happens to be. Every website lives somewhere permanently, on what's called an origin server, which is the original computer storing the real, complete copy of all the files. Sending every single request across the world to that one server would be slow, especially for someone far away. So a content delivery network places many extra copies of the same files on servers scattered around the globe, called edge locations, because they sit at the "edge," close to where people actually are. When a request comes in, it gets routed to the nearest edge location instead of the distant origin. If that nearby copy already has the needed file ready to serve, that's called a cache hit, and the page loads almost instantly. Think of it like a chain of neighborhood libraries that each keep popular books in stock, so most readers never have to travel to the one central warehouse across the country. Only when a file is missing or outdated does the edge location have to fetch a fresh copy from the origin server, which takes a bit longer but happens rarely. This system keeps things fast, reduces strain on the origin server, and keeps services running smoothly even during traffic surges.

| Term | Plain meaning | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| Origin server | The original computer holding the master copy of a website's files | It's the ultimate source of truth everything else copies from |
| Edge location | A nearby server holding a copy of popular content | It lets requests be answered close by, cutting wait time |
| Cache hit | When a nearby copy already has the requested file | It means near-instant loading with no long trip needed |
| Content delivery network | The whole system of connected edge locations working together | It keeps websites fast and reliable for people everywhere |
